newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's Khan on slippery political wicket.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's Khan on slippery political wicket.

text.p: Dashing and hugely popular, former cricket hero Imran Khan has enviable political appeal but faces an uphill battle in his quest to become Pakistan's next prime minister, analysts said on Saturday.
Khan launched his campaign on Friday, saying his seven-month-old political movement would clean up rampant corruption and stand up to foreign interests.
President Farooq Leghari called general elections for February after sacking former prime minister Benazir Bhutto on Tuesday over disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
Khan is a household name in cricket-crazy Pakistan. He won the hearts of his countrymen when he skippered Pakistan to victory in the 1992 World Cup.
After retiring from sport, he raised enough funds to build a cancer hospital in his hometown of Lahore.
His glamorous marriage last year to Jemima Goldsmith, daughter of Anglo-French financier Sir James Goldsmith, made waves in Islamic Pakistan but won him international publicity.

Khan said most Pakistanis had accepted the fact that he had married a foreigner, but that some critics had tried to turn his wife's religious background against him. Jemima was Jewish before converting to Islam.
"There is a campaign to make it out to be a Jewish conspiracy. How much that affects, I don't know," he said.
For a long time Khan, 43, denied any ambition to become prime minister.
But in April he launched his Tehreek-i-Insaaf movement that he said would sweep away a corrupt political class and redeem a nation he said had lost its self-esteem.
"The time has come for new people," he said on Friday at a news conference that drew at least as many foreign as local journalists.
Local newspapers devoted only modest coverage to Khan's announcement, a reflection of the scepticism his campaign has generated.
Bhutto, with characteristic candor, belittled Khan's prospects earlier in the week.
"As far as the country is concerned, there are two parties, the others are bit players. There are many bit players, he (Khan) is one," Bhutto told Reuters Television on Thursday.
Khan acknowledged that he would have preferred more time to gear up for elections, which would have been held in 1998 if Bhutto had served out her term.
"No doubt, elections are early for us," he said.
Ahmed Rashid, a columnist with The Nation newspaper, said Khan would benefit from the political turmoil and deep-seated frustration with corruption.
"But I don't think he will do very well in this election," Rashid said. "He is attracting very young people to his rallies but not adults. Many are there just out of curiosity."

Ayaz Amir, a columnist with the Dawn newspaper, agreed. "He is not very strongly placed at the moment. He has no nationwide organisation and is still cutting his political teeth. His chances are very, very slim."
Najam Sethi, editor of the Friday Times, said Khan would do well in urban areas, drawing supporters from the Pakistan Muslim League (PML) headed by former prime minister Nawaz Sharif.
"Imran Khan should give Nawaz Sharif a run for his money," Sethi said, adding that if the elections were postponed beyond February 3, as some have predicted, "he could do very well".
Rashid said Khan's platform would appeal mainly to conservative, religious voters -- traditionally the PML's vote bank. "He would strip Sharif's vote," he said.
